Weak null singularities in general relativity

Jonathan Luk Address: Department of Mathematics, Stanford University, Stanford CA 94305-2125, USA Email address: jluk@stanford.edu
Abstract.

We construct a class of spacetimes (without symmetry assumptions) satisfying the vacuum Einstein equations with singular boundaries on two null hypersurfaces intersecting in the future on a 2-sphere. The metric of these spacetimes extends continuously beyond the singularities while the Christoffel symbols fail to be square integrable in a neighborhood of any point on the singular boundaries. The construction shows moreover that the singularities are stable in a suitable sense. These singularities are stronger than the impulsive gravitational spacetimes considered by Luk-Rodnianski and conjecturally they are present in the interior of generic black holes arising from gravitational collapse.

1. Introduction

In this paper, we study the existence and stability of weak null singularities in general relativity without symmetry assumptions. More precisely, a weak null singularity is a singular null boundary of a spacetime (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) solving the Einstein equations

R​i​cμ​ν−12​R​gμ​ν=Tμ​νRic_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}Rg_{\mu\nu}=T_{\mu\nu}

such that the Christoffel symbols blow up and are not square integrable while the metric is continuous up to the boundary. This can be interpreted as a terminal singularity of the spacetime as it cannot be made sense of as a weak solution11 1 One can define a weak solution to the Einstein equations by requiring ∫ℳR​i​c​(X,Y)−12​R​g​(X,Y)−T⁡(X,Y)​𝑑V​o​l=0\int_{\mathcal{M}}Ric(X,Y)-\frac{1}{2}Rg(X,Y)-T(X,Y)dVol=0 in the weak sense for all compactly supported smooth vector fields XX and YY. After integration by parts, the minimal regularity required for the spacetime for this to be defined is that the Christoffel symbols are square-integrable. See the discussion on p.13 of [5]. to the Einstein equations along the singular boundary. While the singularity is sufficiently strong to be terminal, it is at the same time sufficiently weak such that the metric in an appropriate coordinate system is continuous up to the boundary.

The study of weak null singularities began with the attempts to understand the (in)stability of the Cauchy horizon in the black hole interior of Reissner-Nordström spacetimes. Reissner-Nordström spacetimes are the unique two-parameter family of asymptotically flat (with two ends), spherically symmetric, static solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell equations. Their Penrose diagrams22 2 for 0<|Q|<M0<{|Q|}<M are given by Figure 1. As seen in the Penrose diagram, the Reissner-Nordström solution possesses a smooth Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+} in the interior of the black hole such that the spacetime can be extended non-uniquely as a smooth solution to the Einstein-Maxwell system. This feature is also shared33 3 for 0<|a|<M0<|a|<M by the Kerr family of solutions to the vacuum Einstein equations, which can also be depicted by a Penrose diagram given by Figure 1. According to the strong cosmic censorship conjecture (see Section 1.1 below), the Reissner-Nordström and Kerr spacetimes are expected to be non-generic and the smooth Cauchy horizons are expected to be unstable.

In a seminal work, Dafermos [7, 8] showed that for a spacetime solution to the spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell-real scalar field system, if an appropriate upper and lower bound for the scalar field is assumed on the event horizon, then in a neighborhood of timelike infinity, the black hole terminates in a weak null singularity. The necessary upper bound was shown to hold for non-extremal black hole spacetimes arising from asymptotically flat initial data by Dafermos-Rodnianski [10]. In particular, this implies that near timelike infinity, the terminal boundary of the Cauchy development does not contain a spacelike portion.

In a more recent work [9], Dafermos showed that if, in addition to assuming the two black hole exterior regions settle to Reissner-Nordström with appropriate rates, the initial data are moreover globally close to that of Reissner-Nordström, then the maximal Cauchy development of the data possesses the same Penrose diagram as Reissner-Nordström. In particular, the spacetime terminates in a global bifurcate weak null singularity and the singular boundary does not contain any spacelike portion.

The works [7, 8, 9] were in part motivated by the physics literature on the instability of Cauchy horizons, weak null singularities and the strong cosmic censorship conjecture. It will be discussed below in Section 1.1.

While the works of Dafermos [7, 8, 9] are restricted to the class of spherically symmetric spacetimes, they nonetheless suggest the genericity of weak null singularities in the black hole interior, at least “in a neighborhood of timelike infinity”. In particular, they motivate the following conjecture for the vacuum Einstein equations

If Conjecture 1 is true, then in particular there exist local stable weak null singularities for the vacuum Einstein equations without symmetry assumptions. We show in this paper that there is in fact a large class of such singularities, parameterized by singular initial data. More specifically, we solve a characteristic initial value problem with singular initial data and construct a class of stable bifurcate weak null singularities.

To motivate the strength of the singularity considered in this paper, we first recall the strength of the spherically symmetric weak null singularities in a neighborhood of Reissner-Nordström studied in [8]. The instability of the Reissner-Nordström Cauchy horizon is in fact already suggested by a linear analysis (see [4, 20, 23]). Remark 1.

This class of stable local weak null singularities that we construct in particular provides the first construction of weak null singularities of such strength for the vacuum Einstein equations.77 7 We recall the Birkhoff’s Theorem which states that the only spherically symmetric vacuum spacetimes are the Minkowski and Schwarzschild solutions. Thus to construct stable examples of weak null singularities in vacuum, one necessarily works outside the class of spherically symmetric spacetimes.

In that context, we can in fact combine the methods in this paper with that in [17] to show that the domain of existence can be extended so that only one of the characteristic length scales is required to be small. We will omit the details of the proof of this result.

Theorem 1, which proves the existence and stability of the conjecturally generic weak null singularities, can be viewed as a first step towards Conjecture 1. A next step is an analogue of [8] for the vacuum Einstein equations without symmetry assumptions, i.e., to solve the characteristic initial value problem inside the black hole with data prescribed on the event horizon that is approaching Kerr at appropriate rates. This requires an understanding of the formation of weak null singularities from smooth data on the event horizon (see part (1) of Conjecture 1). A full resolution of Conjecture 1.2, however, requires in addition an understanding of the decay rates of gravitational radiation along the event horizon for generic perturbations of Kerr spacetime. This latter problem is intimately tied to the problem of the nonlinear stability of Kerr spacetimes, which continues to be one of the most important and challenging open problems in mathematical general relativity. Nevertheless, significant progress has been made for the corresponding linear problem in the past decade. We refer the readers to the survey of Dafermos-Rodnianski [11] for more about this linear problem.

The approach for the main theorem applies equally well to the Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system without symmetry assumptions88 8 This can be easily seen by decomposing the Maxwell field and the gradient of the scalar field in terms of the null frame below. The components in this decomposition obey equations that can be put in the same schematic form as in Section 2.4. Therefore, the Maxwell field and the scalar field and their derivatives satisfy estimates similar to those for the Ricci coefficients and curvature components.. Thus, we show that the weak null singularity of Dafermos [8], which arises from appropriately decaying data on the event horizon, is stable against non-spherically symmetric perturbations on the hypersurface Σ\Sigma sufficiently far within the black hole region (see Figure 5).

1.1. Weak Null Singularities and Strong Cosmic Censorship Conjecture

The study of weak null singularities can be viewed in the larger context of Penrose’s celebrated strong cosmic censorship conjecture in general relativity. The conjecture states that for generic asymptotically flat initial data for “reasonable” Einstein-matter systems, the maximal Cauchy development is future inextendible as a suitably regular Lorentzian manifold. This would guarantee general relativity to be a deterministic theory.

As pointed out above, the Kerr and Reissner-Nordström families of solutions (of the Einstein vacuum and Einstein-Maxwell equations respectively) have maximal Cauchy developments that are extendible as larger smooth spacetimes unless the angular momentum or the charge vanishes. This is connected with the existence of a smooth Cauchy horizon in the black hole interior such that the spacetime can be extended beyond as a smooth solution. According to the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, this is expected to be non-generic.

On the other hand, the situation for the Schwarzschild spacetime is more preferable from the point of view of the deterministic nature of the theory. The maximal development of the Schwarzschild spacetime terminates with a spacelike singularity at which the Hawking mass and the curvature scalar invariants blow up. In particular, the spacetime cannot be extended in C2C^{2}.

The early motivation for the strong cosmic censorship conjecture besides the desirability of a deterministic theory is a linear heuristic argument by Penrose [23] suggesting that the Reissner-Nordström Cauchy horizon is unstable. This was also confirmed by the numerical work by Simpson and Penrose [27]. It is thus conjectured that a small global perturbation would lead to a singularity in the interior of the black hole in such a way that the maximal Cauchy development is future inextendible.

However, the nature of the singular boundary in the interior of black holes was not well-understood99 9 In particular, it was believed that a perturbation of the Reissner-Nordström Cauchy horizon would lead to a Schwarzschild type singularity. until the first study of weak null singularity carried out by Hiscock [12]. In an attempt to understand the instability of the Reissner-Nordström Cauchy horizon, he considered the Vaidya model allowing for a self-gravitating ingoing null dust. In this model, an explicit solution can be found and he showed that various components of the Christoffel symbols blow up. This, however, was called a whimper singularity as the Hawking mass and the curvature scalar invariants remain bounded.

In subsequent works, Poisson-Israel [25, 26] added an outgoing null dust to the model considered by Hiscock. While explicit solutions were not available, they were able to deduce that the second outgoing null dust would cause the Hawking mass to blow up at the null singularity. It was then thought of as a stronger singularity than that of Hiscock.

However, from the point of view of partial differential equations, it is more natural to view this singularity at the level of the non-square-integrability of the Christoffel symbols, which is exactly the threshold such that the spacetime cannot be defined as a weak solution to the Einstein equations. From this perspective, the singularity of Poisson-Israel is as strong as that of Hiscock and both singularities can be viewed as terminal boundaries for the spacetimes in question.

While the Christoffel symbols blow up at the Cauchy horizon, one can also think that the Cauchy horizon is “stable” in the sense that no singularity arises before the “original Cauchy horizon”. In particular, there is no spacelike portion of the singular boundary in a neighborhood of timelike infinity. This is thus contrary to the case of the Schwarzschild spacetime. This weak null singularity picture has been further explored and justified in many numerical works (see [1, 2, 3]).

As we described before, the aforementioned picture of the interior of black holes was finally established by Dafermos in the context of the spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell-scalar field system [7]. This is the main motivation for our present work in which we initiate the study of weak null singularities of similar strength in vacuum without any symmetry assumptions.

Finally, we note that a class of analytic spacetimes with slightly weaker singularities have been previously constructed in [22]. While this class of spacetime is more restrictive, as discussed in [22], it nonetheless admits the full “functional degrees of freedom” of the Einstein equations.

1.2. Comparison with Impulsive Gravitational Waves

As pointed out by Dafermos [9], the weak null singularities that we consider in this paper share many similarities with impulsive gravitational waves. The latter are vacuum spacetimes admitting null hypersurfaces which support delta function singularities in the Riemann curvature tensor. Explicit examples were first constructed by Penrose [24], Khan-Penrose [14] and Szekeres [28]. In these spacetimes, while the Christoffel symbols are not continuous, they remain bounded. Therefore, in contrast with the weak null singularities that we consider here, these impulsive gravitational waves are not terminal singularities. In fact, the solution to the vacuum Einstein equation extends beyond the singularity and is smooth except across the singular hypersurface. Nevertheless, both scenarios represent singularities propagating along null hypersurfaces and from a mathematical point of view, the proofs of the existence theory for these singularities share many common features.

In recent joint works with Rodnianski [19, 18], we initiated the rigorous mathematical study for general impulsive gravitational waves without symmetry assumptions. We constructed the impulsive gravitational waves via solving the characteristic initial problem such that the initial data admit curvature delta singularities supported on an embedded 2-sphere. One of the new ideas in the proof is the use of renormalized energy estimates for the curvature components, i.e., instead of controlling the spacetime curvature components in L2L^{2}, we subtract off an L∞L^{\infty} correction from some curvature components. This allowed us to derive a closed system of L2L^{2} estimates which is completely independent of the singular curvature components.

In [18], when the interaction of impulsive gravitational waves was studied, we also extended the analysis to include a class of spacetimes such that when measured in the worst direction, the Christoffel symbols are merely in L2L^{2}. We proved an existence and uniqueness theorem for spacetimes with such low regularity and showed that the spacetime solution can be extended beyond the singularities. Notice that this result is in fact sharp: This is because if the Christoffel symbols fail to be square-integrable, the spacetime cannot be extended as a weak solution to the Einstein equations (see footnote 1).

By contrast, the spacetimes considered in this paper have Christoffel symbols which are1010 10 In fact, we allow initial data to be in LpL^{p} only for p=1p=1, but not for any p>1p>1. not in L2L^{2}. Even though the weak null singularities are terminal singularities in the sense that there cannot be an existence theory beyond them, the theory developed in [19, 18] can be extended to control the spacetime up to the singularity. Moreover, our main theorem, which allows for two weak null singularities terminating at their intersection, can be viewed as an extension of the result in [18] on the interaction of two impulsive gravitational waves. In particular, the renormalized energy of [19, 18] plays an important role in the proof of our main theorem. However, even after renormalization, the renormalized curvature is still singular (i.e., not in L2L^{2}) and has to be dealt with using an additional weighted estimate.

1.4. Main Ideas of the Proof

All the known proofs of regularity for the Einstein equations without symmetry assumptions rely on L2L^{2} estimates on the metric and its derivatives or the Riemann curvature tensor and its derivatives. Let us denote schematically by Γ\Gamma a general Ricci coefficient and by Ψ\Psi a general curvature component decomposed with respect to a null frame adapted to the double null foliation. In the double null foliation gauge (see for example, [15, 5]), the standard approach to obtain a priori bounds is to couple the L2L^{2} estimates for the curvature components

∫HΨ2+∫H¯Ψ2≤Data +∬Γ​Ψ​Ψ\int_{H}\Psi^{2}+\int_{\underline{H}}\Psi^{2}\leq\mbox{ Data }+\iint\Gamma\Psi\Psi

with the estimates for the Ricci coefficients obtained using the transport equations

∇3Γ=Ψ+Γ​Γ,\nabla_{3}\Gamma=\Psi+\Gamma\Gamma,
∇4Γ=Ψ+Γ​Γ.\nabla_{4}\Gamma=\Psi+\Gamma\Gamma.

However, in the setting of two weak null singularities, none of the spacetime curvature components α,β,ρ,σ,β¯,α¯\alpha,\beta,\rho,\sigma,\underline{\beta},\underline{\alpha} are in L2L^{2}!

Nevertheless, while these curvature components are singular, the nature of their singularity is specific. More precisely, while the spacetime curvature components ρ\rho and σ\sigma are not in L2L^{2}, they can be written as a sum of some regular intrinsic curvature components KK and σˇ\check{\sigma} (see further discussion in Section 1.4.1) which belong to L2L^{2} and terms which are quadratic in Γ\Gamma. We therefore prove L2L^{2} estimates for KK and σˇ\check{\sigma}, which we will call the “renormalized curvature components” (see [19, 18]). Moreover, by considering (K,σˇ)(K,\check{\sigma}) instead of (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma), we remove all appearances of α\alpha and α¯\underline{\alpha} in the estimates and so that we do not have to deal with the singularities of α\alpha and α¯\underline{\alpha}! It still remains to control the singular curvature components β\beta and β¯\underline{\beta}. Here, we make use of the fact that β\beta and β¯\underline{\beta} are singular in a specific manner towards the singular boundary H¯u¯∗\underline{H}_{\underline{u}_{*}} and Hu∗H_{u_{*}} respectively. We therefore introduce degenerate L2L^{2} norms that incorporate these singularities. We will explain the renormalization and the degenerate estimates in more detail below.

1.4.1. Renormalized Energy Estimates

As described above, a main ingredient of the proof of the main theorem is the renormalized energy estimates introduced in [19, 18] in the study of impulsive gravitational waves. This can be seen as follows. For the class of weak null singularities that we consider, while the ℒ/L{\mathcal{L}}\mkern-10.0mu/\,_{L} derivative of the spacetime metric blows up, the metric restricted to the 22-sphere remains regular in the angular directions. Since the Gauss curvature KK is intrinsic to the 22-spheres, it remains bounded. On the other hand, by the Gauss equation:

K=−ρ+12​χ^⋅χ¯^−14​tr​χ​tr​χ¯K=-{\rho}+\frac{1}{2}\hat{\chi}\cdot\hat{\underline{\chi}}-\frac{1}{4}\mbox{tr}\chi\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}

and the fact that tr​χ\mbox{tr}\chi and χ^\hat{\chi} blow up at u¯=u¯∗\underline{u}=\underline{u}_{*}, ρ\rho also blows up at u¯=u¯∗\underline{u}=\underline{u}_{*}. In view of this, we estimate the Gauss curvature KK instead of the spacetime curvature component ρ\rho.

Indeed, we see that the Gauss curvature KK satisfies equations such that the right hand side contains terms that are less singular than the terms in the corresponding equation for ρ\rho. More precisely, for the curvature component ρ\rho, we have (up to lower order terms) the Bianchi equation

∇4ρ+32​tr​χ​ρ=div ​β−12​χ¯^⋅α+…,\nabla_{4}\rho+\frac{3}{2}\mbox{tr}\chi\rho=\mbox{div }\beta-\frac{1}{2}\hat{\underline{\chi}}\cdot\alpha+...,

which contains the non-integrable curvature component α\alpha. On the other hand, the Gauss curvature obeys the equation (see (12))

∇4K+tr​χ​K=−div ​β+…,\nabla_{4}K+\mbox{tr}\chi K=-\mbox{div }\beta+...,

where there are no terms containing α\alpha or are quadratic in tr​χ\mbox{tr}\chi, χ^\hat{\chi} and ω\omega, i.e. every term on the right hand side of the equation is integrable in the u¯\underline{u} direction1313 13 The can be compared with the renormalization introduced in [19] and [18], where we estimated ρˇ=ρ−12​χ^⋅χ¯^\check{\rho}=\rho-\frac{1}{2}\hat{\chi}\cdot\hat{\underline{\chi}} instead of ρ\rho. Whereas the renormalization using ρˇ\check{\rho} allows one to eliminate α\alpha in the estimates, it nonetheless introduces a term 14​tr​χ¯​|χ^|2\frac{1}{4}\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}|\hat{\chi}|^{2}, which is not integrable in the u¯\underline{u} direction in the setting of the present paper. Instead, by studying the equation for KK, we see none of these terms which are quadratic in tr​χ\mbox{tr}\chi, χ^\hat{\chi} or ω\omega! This fact can also be derived directly by considering the equations for ∇4K\nabla_{4}K using the intrinsic definition of the Gauss curvature..

In a similar fashion, by considering the renormalized curvature component1414 14 This is in fact related to the intrinsic curvature of the normal bundle to Su,u¯S_{u,\underline{u}}.

σˇ:=σ+12​χ¯^∧χ^\check{\sigma}:=\sigma+\frac{1}{2}\hat{\underline{\chi}}\wedge\hat{\chi}

instead of σ\sigma, we see that it satisfies an equation such that all the terms on the right hand side are integrable in the u¯\underline{u} direction.

One consequence of the renormalization is that we have completely removed the appearances of the curvature component α\alpha in the equations. In fact, as in [19, 18], this allows us to derive a set of estimates for the renormalized curvature component without requiring any information on the curvature component α\alpha.

Moreover, when considering the equations for ∇3K\nabla_{3}K and ∇3σˇ\nabla_{3}\check{\sigma} for the renormalized curvature components, one sees that α¯\underline{\alpha} does not appear and all the terms are integrable in the uu direction. Therefore, although α\alpha or α¯\underline{\alpha} can be very singular near one of the singular boundaries, we do not need to derive any estimates for them!

1.4.2. Degenerate L2L^{2} Estimates

Since the renormalization above deals with the singularity in the ρ\rho and σ\sigma components and avoids any information on α\alpha and α¯\underline{\alpha}, it remains to derive appropriate L2L^{2} estimates for β\beta and β¯\underline{\beta}.

The main observation is that while β\beta and β¯\underline{\beta} are both singular and fail to be in L2L^{2}, their singularities can be captured quantitatively. Consider the curvature component β\beta. Since the blow up rate of tr​χ\mbox{tr}\chi and χ^\hat{\chi} can be bounded above by f​(u¯)−2f(\underline{u})^{-2}, in view of the Codazzi equations in (10), β\beta is also bounded above by f​(u¯)−2f(\underline{u})^{-2}. In particular, while β\beta is only in Lu¯1L^{1}_{\underline{u}} but not in Lu¯pL^{p}_{\underline{u}} for any p>1p>1, the assumptions on the initial data allow us to control f⁡(u¯)​βf(\underline{u})\beta in Lu¯2L^{2}_{\underline{u}}. We will thus incorporate this blow up in the norms and will be able to still use an L2L^{2} based estimate.

The energy estimates will be obtained directly from two sets of Bianchi equations instead of using the Bel-Robinson tensor. Notice that since the energy estimates for K,σˇK,\check{\sigma} are obtained either together with that for β\beta or that for β¯\underline{\beta}, even though KK and σˇ\check{\sigma} are regular, their energy estimates degenerate. Therefore, at the highest level of derivatives, we have to contend with the weaker L2L^{2} estimates for these curvature components.

A potentially more serious challenge is that the introduction of the degenerate weights in uu and u¯\underline{u} would create terms that cannot be estimated by the energy estimates themselves. Nevertheless, since the weights are chosen to be decreasing towards the future, these uncontrollable terms in fact possess a good sign.

1.4.3. Estimates for the Ricci Coefficients

As indicated above, the Ricci coefficients enter as error terms in the energy estimates. Thus, to close all the estimates, we need to control the Ricci coefficients Γ\Gamma by using the transport equations which in turn have the curvature components in the source terms. Since the various Ricci coefficients have different singular behavior, we separate them according to the bounds that they obey. More precisely, denote by ψH\psi_{H} the components that behave like f​(u¯)−2f(\underline{u})^{-2} as u¯→u¯∗\underline{u}\to\underline{u}_{*}; by ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}} the components that behave like f​(u)−2f(u)^{-2} as u→u∗u\to u_{*}; and by ψ\psi the components that are bounded.

For the singular Ricci coefficients ψH\psi_{H}, we have the following schematic transport equations:

∇3ψH=K+∇ψ+ψ​ψ+ψH¯​ψH.\nabla_{3}\psi_{H}=K+\nabla\psi+\psi\psi+\psi_{\underline{H}}\psi_{H}.

The first three terms on the right hand side of this equation are bounded while the last term is singular. Nevertheless, the singularity of ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}} still allows it to be controlled in L1L^{1} along the e3e_{3} direction. Thus, this equation can be integrated to show that the initial (singular) bounds for ψH\psi_{H} can be propagated. It is important that the terms of the form ψH​ψH\psi_{H}\psi_{H} and ψH¯​ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}}\psi_{\underline{H}} do not appear in the equations. A similar structure can also be seen in the equation for the other singular Ricci coefficients ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}}, which takes the form

∇4ψH¯=K+∇ψ+ψ​ψ+ψH¯​ψH.\nabla_{4}\psi_{\underline{H}}=K+\nabla\psi+\psi\psi+\psi_{\underline{H}}\psi_{H}.

For the regular Ricci coefficients ψ\psi, we have transport equations of the form

∇4ψ=β+ψ​ψH,or∇3ψ=β¯+ψ​ψH¯.\nabla_{4}\psi=\beta+\psi\psi_{H},\quad\mbox{or}\quad\nabla_{3}\psi=\underline{\beta}+\psi\psi_{\underline{H}}.

The bounds that we prove show that the right hand side is integrable and therefore ψ\psi remains bounded. For example, in the ∇4\nabla_{4} equation, it is important that we do not have terms of the form ψH​ψH\psi_{H}\psi_{H}, ψ​ψH¯\psi\psi_{\underline{H}}, ψH​ψH¯\psi_{H}\psi_{\underline{H}} and ψH¯​ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}}\psi_{\underline{H}}, which are not uniformly bounded after integrating along the e4e_{4} direction.

1.4.4. Null Structure in the Energy Estimates

A priori, the degenerate L2L^{2} estimates that we introduce may not be sufficient to control the error terms. Nevertheless, the vacuum Einstein equations possess a remarkable null structure which allows one to close the estimates using only the degenerate L2L^{2} estimates.

For example, in the energy estimates for the singular component β\beta, we have

‖f⁡(u¯)​β‖L2​(H)2≤Data +‖f2​(u¯)​(β​ψH¯​β+β​ψH​β¯+β​ψ​K)‖Lu1​Lu¯1​L1​(S).||f(\underline{u})\beta||_{L^{2}(H)}^{2}\leq\mbox{ Data }+||f^{2}(\underline{u})(\beta\psi_{\underline{H}}\beta+\beta\psi_{H}\underline{\beta}+\beta\psi K)||_{L^{1}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{1}(S)}.

To estimate the first term, it suffices to note that ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}}, while singular, can be shown to be small after integrating along the uu direction. Thus the first term can be controlled using Gronwall’s inequality. For the second term, since the singularity for β\beta has the same strength as that for ψH\psi_{H} (and similarly the singularity for β¯\underline{\beta} has the same strength as that for ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}}), the singularity in this term is similar to that in the first term and can also be bounded. The final term is less singular since ψ\psi and KK are both uniformly bounded.1515 15 Although as pointed out before, the highest derivative estimates for KK in the energy norm suffer a loss as one approaches the singular boundaries, this term can nevertheless be controlled. Notice that if other combinations of curvature terms and Ricci coefficients such as β​ψH​β\beta\psi_{H}\beta, β​ψH¯​β¯\beta\psi_{\underline{H}}\underline{\beta} or β​ψH​K\beta\psi_{H}K appear in the error terms, the degenerate energy will not be strong enough to close the bounds!

In order to close all the estimates, we need to commute also with higher derivatives. As in [19, 18], we will only commute with angular covariant derivatives. These commutations will not introduce terms that are more singular. Moreover, the null structure of the estimates indicated above is also preserved under these commutations.

Similar to [19, 18], the renormalization introduces error terms in the energy estimates such that the Ricci coefficients have one more derivative compared to the curvature components. These terms cannot be estimated via transport equations alone but are controlled using also elliptic estimates on the spheres. A form of null structure similar to that described above also makes an appearance in these elliptic estimates, allowing all the bounds to be closed.

1.5. Outline of the Paper

We end the introduction with an outline of the remainder of the paper. In Section 2, we introduce the basic setup of the paper, including the double null foliation, the coordinate system and the Einstein vacuum equations recast in terms of the geometric quantities associated to the double null foliation. In Section 3, we introduce the norms used in the paper and state a theorem on a priori estimates (Theorem 5) which imply our main existence theorem (Theorem 2). In Section 4, we construct a class of characteristic initial data satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 2. In Sections 5-8, we prove Theorem 5. In Section 5, we obtain the estimates for the metric components and derive functional inequalities useful in our setting. Then in Sections 6 and 7, we prove bounds for the Ricci coefficients assuming control of the curvature components. In Section 8, we close all the estimates by obtaining bounds for the curvature components. Finally, in Section 9, we discuss the nature of the singular boundary and prove Theorems 3 and 4.

We will recast the Einstein equations as a system for Ricci coefficients and curvature components associated to a null frame e3e_{3}, e4e_{4} defined above and an orthonormal frame1717 17 Of course the orthonormal frame is only defined locally. 3. Norms

In this section, we define the norms that we will use to control the geometric quantities. We will in particular use the schematic notation defined in Section 2.4. Our norms will be of the form Lup​Lu¯q​Lr​(S)L^{p}_{u}L^{q}_{\underline{u}}L^{r}(S), where LupL^{p}_{u} and Lu¯qL^{q}_{\underline{u}} are defined with respect to the measures d​udu and d​u¯d\underline{u} respectively and Lr​(S)L^{r}(S) is defined for any tensors ϕ\phi on Su,u¯S_{u,\underline{u}} by

‖ϕ‖Lr​(Su,u¯):=(∫Su,u¯(ϕA1​A2​…​An​ϕA1​A2​…​An)r2)1r,\|\phi\|_{L^{r}(S_{u,\underline{u}})}:=\left(\int_{S_{u,\underline{u}}}(\phi_{A_{1}A_{2}...A_{n}}\phi^{A_{1}A_{2}...A_{n}})^{\frac{r}{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{r}},

where the integral is with respect to the volume form induced by γ\gamma.

We define the following norms for the Ricci coefficients ψ\psi for p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}:

𝒪i,p​[ψ]:=‖∇iψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​Lp​(S).\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi]:=||\nabla^{i}\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{p}(S)}. (14)

Define the following norms for the Ricci coefficients ψH\psi_{H} for p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}:

𝒪i,p​[ψH]:=‖f⁡(u¯)​∇iψH‖Lu¯2​Lu∞​Lp​(S).\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{H}]:=||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{i}\psi_{H}||_{L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}_{u}L^{p}(S)}. (15)

Similarly, we define the following norms for the Ricci coefficients ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}} for p∈[1,∞]p\in[1,\infty], i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}:

𝒪i,p​[ψH¯]:=‖f⁡(u)​∇iψH¯‖Lu2​Lu¯∞​Lp​(S).\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{\underline{H}}]:=||f(u)\nabla^{i}\psi_{\underline{H}}||_{L^{2}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{p}(S)}. (16)

As a shorthand, we define the following norm combining all of the norms above:

𝒪i,p:=∑ψ∈{η,η¯}𝒪i,p​[ψ]+∑ψH∈{t​r​χ,χ^,ω}𝒪i,p​[ψH]+∑ψH¯∈{t​r​χ¯,χ¯^,ω¯}𝒪i,p​[ψH¯].\mathcal{O}_{i,p}:=\sum_{\psi\in\{\eta,\underline{\eta}\}}\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi]+\sum_{\psi_{H}\in\{tr\chi,\hat{\chi},\omega\}}\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{H}]+\sum_{\psi_{\underline{H}}\in\{tr\underline{\chi},\hat{\underline{\chi}},\underline{\omega}\}}\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{\underline{H}}].

We make two remarks concerning these norms:

Remark 7.

While the norms for ψH\psi_{H} and ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}} are based on L2L^{2} in u¯\underline{u} and uu respectively, by virtue of the weights f⁡(u¯)f(\underline{u}) and f⁡(u)f(u), they actually control the L1L^{1} norms. More precisely, since ∫0u¯∗1f2​(u¯′)​d​u¯′<ϵ2\int_{0}^{\underline{u}_{*}}\frac{1}{f^{2}(\underline{u}^{\prime})}d\underline{u}^{\prime}<\epsilon^{{2}} and ∫0u∗1f2​(u′)​d​u′<ϵ2\int_{0}^{u_{*}}\frac{1}{f^{2}(u^{\prime})}du^{\prime}<\epsilon^{{2}}, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have

‖∇iψH‖Lu¯1​Lu∞​Lp​(S)≤C​ϵ​𝒪i,p​[ψH],||\nabla^{i}\psi_{H}||_{L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}_{u}L^{p}(S)}\leq C\epsilon\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{H}],

and

‖∇iψH¯‖Lu1​Lu¯∞​Lp​(S)≤C​ϵ​𝒪i,p​[ψH¯].||\nabla^{i}\psi_{\underline{H}}||_{L^{1}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{p}(S)}\leq C\epsilon\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{\underline{H}}].
Remark 8.

The norm 𝒪i,p​[ψH]\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{H}] (resp. 𝒪i,p​[ψH¯]\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{\underline{H}}]) allows us to first take L∞L^{\infty} along the uu direction (resp. u¯\underline{u} direction) before the L2L^{2} norm in u¯\underline{u} (resp. uu) is taken. This is stronger than the norms such that the order is reversed, i.e., we have

‖f⁡(u¯)​∇iψH‖Lu∞​Lu¯2​Lp​(S)≤C​𝒪i,p​[ψH],||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{i}\psi_{H}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{p}(S)}\leq C\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{H}],

and

‖f⁡(u)​∇iψH¯‖Lu¯∞​Lu¯2​Lp​(S)≤C​𝒪i,p​[ψH¯].||f(u)\nabla^{i}\psi_{\underline{H}}||_{L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{p}(S)}\leq C\mathcal{O}_{i,p}[\psi_{\underline{H}}].

In addition to the above norms, we need to define norms for the highest derivatives for the Ricci coefficients. Let

𝒪~4,2:=‖f​(u¯)2​∇4tr​χ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S)+||f​(u)2​∇4tr​χ¯||Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S)+‖f⁡(u¯)​∇4(χ^,ω)‖Lu∞​Lu¯2​L2​(S)+||f⁡(u)​∇4(η,η¯)||Lu∞​Lu¯2​L2​(S)+‖f⁡(u)​∇4(χ¯^,ω¯)‖Lu¯∞​Lu2​L2​(S)+||f⁡(u¯)​∇4(η,η¯)||Lu¯∞​Lu2​L2​(S).\begin{split}\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{4,2}:=&||f(\underline{u})^{2}\nabla^{4}\mbox{tr}\chi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}+||f(u)^{2}\nabla^{4}\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}\\ &+||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{4}(\hat{\chi},\omega)||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}+||f(u)\nabla^{4}(\eta,\underline{\eta})||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}\\ &+||f(u)\nabla^{4}(\hat{\underline{\chi}},\underline{\omega})||_{L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}_{u}L^{2}(S)}+||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{4}(\eta,\underline{\eta})||_{L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}_{u}L^{2}(S)}.\end{split} (17)
Remark 9.

Here, note that for the norms for χ^\hat{\chi}, ω\omega, η\eta, η¯\underline{\eta}, χ¯^\hat{\underline{\chi}} and ω\omega, L∞L^{\infty} in u¯\underline{u} (or uu) is taken after L2L^{2} in uu (or u¯\underline{u}). According to Remark 8, this is weaker than the 𝒪i,2\mathcal{O}_{i,2} norms defined above.

Remark 10.

Notice that the norms for the fourth derivatives of η\eta and η¯\underline{\eta} come with a weight f⁡(u)f(u) or f⁡(u¯)f(\underline{u}). This is in contrast to the lower order derivatives for η\eta and η¯\underline{\eta}, which can be estimated in Lu∞​Lu¯∞L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}} without any degeneration. The degeneration here arises from the fact that these higher order derivatives are recovered from the energy estimates for ∇3K\nabla^{3}K. These energy estimates for ∇3K\nabla^{3}K, which are derived simultaneously with the estimates for the singular components ∇3β\nabla^{3}\beta or ∇3β¯\nabla^{3}\underline{\beta}, have a degeneration either in u¯\underline{u} or uu.

𝒪i​n​i:=∑i≤3(||∇iψ||Lu¯∞​L2​(S0,u¯)+||∇iψ||Lu∞​L2​(Su,0)+||f(u¯)∇iψH||Lu¯2​L2​(S0,u¯)+||f(u)∇iψH¯||Lu2​L2​(Su,0))+‖f​(u¯)2​∇4tr​χ‖Lu¯∞​L2​(S0,u¯)+||f​(u)2​∇4tr​χ¯||Lu∞​L2​(Su,0)+‖∇4tr​χ¯‖Lu¯∞​L2​(S0,u¯)+‖∇4tr​χ‖Lu∞​L2​(Su,0)+‖f⁡(u¯)​∇4(χ^,ω)‖Lu¯2​L2​(S0,u¯)+||∇4(η,η¯)||Lu¯2​L2​(S0,u¯)+‖f⁡(u)​∇4(χ¯^,ω¯)‖Lu2​L2​(Su,0)+||∇4(η,η¯)||Lu2​L2​(Su,0)\begin{split}\mathcal{O}_{ini}:=&\sum_{i\leq 3}\big(||\nabla^{i}\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}+||\nabla^{i}\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}(S_{u,0})}\\ &\quad+||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{i}\psi_{H}||_{L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{{2}}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}+||f(u)\nabla^{i}\psi_{\underline{H}}||_{L^{2}_{u}L^{{2}}(S_{u,0})}\big)\\ &+||f(\underline{u})^{2}\nabla^{4}\mbox{tr}\chi||_{L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}+||f(u)^{2}\nabla^{4}\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}(S_{u,0})}\\ &+||\nabla^{4}\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}||_{L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}+||\nabla^{4}\mbox{tr}\chi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}(S_{u,0})}\\ &+||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{4}(\hat{\chi},\omega)||_{L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}+||\nabla^{4}(\eta,\underline{\eta})||_{L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}\\ &+||f(u)\nabla^{4}(\hat{\underline{\chi}},\underline{\omega})||_{L^{2}_{u}L^{2}(S_{u,0})}+||\nabla^{4}(\eta,\underline{\eta})||_{L^{2}_{u}L^{2}(S_{u,0})}\end{split}

and

In order to prove Theorem 2, we will establish a priori estimates for the geometric quantities in the above norms:

Theorem 5.

Assume that the initial data for the characteristic initial value problem satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 2 with ϵ\epsilon sufficiently small. Then there exists BB depending only on DD and dd such that

∑i≤3𝒪i,2+𝒪~4,2+ℛ≤B.\sum_{i\leq 3}\mathcal{O}_{i,2}+\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{4,2}+\mathcal{R}\leq B.

In the remainder of the paper, we will focus on the proof of Theorem 5 (after constructing initial data sets in the next section). Standard methods show that Theorem 5 implies Theorem 2. We will omit the details and refer the readers to [5, 19] for a proof that the a priori estimates imply the existence theorem.

Remark 11.

The assumptions of Theorem 2 imply the boundedness of the following weighted L2L^{2} norms of the curvature components:

∑i≤3‖f⁡(u¯)​∇iβ‖Lu¯2​L2​(S0,u¯)+∑i≤3‖∇i(K,σˇ)‖Lu¯2​L2​(S0,u¯)≤D~,\sum_{i\leq 3}||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{i}\beta||_{L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}+\sum_{i\leq 3}||{\nabla^{i}(K,\check{\sigma})}||_{L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}\leq\tilde{D},

and

∑i≤3‖f⁡(u)​∇iβ¯‖Lu2​L2​(Su,0)+∑i≤3‖∇i(K,σˇ)‖Lu2​L2​(Su,0)≤D~,\sum_{i\leq 3}||f({u})\nabla^{i}\underline{\beta}||_{L^{2}_{u}L^{2}(S_{u,0})}+\sum_{i\leq 3}||{\nabla^{i}(K,\check{\sigma})}||_{L^{2}_{{u}}L^{2}(S_{u,0})}\leq\tilde{D},

for some D~\tilde{D} depending only on DD and dd. These estimates for β\beta, σˇ\check{\sigma} and β¯\underline{\beta} follow immediately from the constraint equations on the 2-spheres (see (10)). The bound for KK follows after integrating the null Bianchi equations for KK on each of the initial null hypersurfaces (see (12)).2020 20 Notice that it is precisely for the initial bound for KK that we require an extra derivative for χ\chi on H0H_{0} (and χ¯\underline{\chi} on H¯0\underline{H}_{0}) in the assumptions of the theorem. This is related to the intrinsic loss of derivatives for the characteristic initial value problem for second order hyperbolic systems (see [21]). In particular, the assumptions of Theorem 2 imply that

𝒪i​n​i+ℛi​n​i≤D~.\mathcal{O}_{ini}+\mathcal{R}_{ini}\leq\tilde{D}.

∑i≤N−2|∇iK|γ≲1.\sum_{i\leq N-2}|\nabla^{i}K|_{\gamma}\lesssim 1.

On H0H_{0}, since Ω=1\Omega=1, η=ζ\eta=\zeta. Thus combining the transport equation for ζ\zeta in (9) and the Codazzi equation for β\beta in (10) and rewriting in ℒ/{\mathcal{L}}\mkern-10.0mu/\, (instead of ∇4\nabla_{4}), we have

ℒ/∂∂u¯ζ+trχζ=div χ−∇trχ.{\mathcal{L}}\mkern-10.0mu/\,_{\frac{\partial}{\partial\underline{u}}}\zeta+\mbox{tr}\chi\zeta=\mbox{div }\chi-\nabla\mbox{tr}\chi.

Recall from (25) that the initial data for ζ\zeta and its angular derivatives are bounded. Therefore, by the estimates for tr​χ\mbox{tr}\chi and χ^\hat{\chi} (and their angular derivatives) above, we have

∑|J|≤N−1|(∂∂θ)J​ζ|≲1.\sum_{|J|\leq N-1}|\big(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\big)^{J}\zeta|\lesssim 1.

The bounds for the metric and Christoffel symbols on the sphere imply

∑j≤N−1‖∇jζ‖Lu¯∞​L∞​(S0,u¯)≲1\sum_{j\leq N-1}||\nabla^{j}\zeta||_{L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}\lesssim 1

as desired.

Estimates for ∇itr​χ¯\nabla^{i}\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}

Similar to ζ\zeta, tr​χ¯\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi} obeys a transport equations along the null generators of H0H_{0}. More precisely, (9) and the Gauss equation in (10) imply that

ℒ/∂∂u¯tr​χ¯+tr​χ​tr​χ¯=−2​K−2​div ​ζ+2​|ζ|2.{\mathcal{L}}\mkern-10.0mu/\,_{\frac{\partial}{\partial\underline{u}}}\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}+\mbox{tr}\chi\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}=-2K-2\mbox{div }\zeta+2|\zeta|^{2}.

Thus, the previous estimates imply

∑j≤N−2‖∇jtr​χ¯‖Lu¯∞​L∞​(S0,u¯)≲1\sum_{j\leq N-2}||\nabla^{j}\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}||_{L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S_{0,\underline{u}})}\lesssim 1

Now, combining all the estimates that we have obtained so far, requiring ff to satisfy

∫0u¯∗f​(u¯)−4​𝑑u¯=∞\int_{0}^{\underline{u}_{*}}f(\underline{u})^{-4}d\underline{u}=\infty

and taking NN to sufficiently large, we have thus constructed initial data set on H0H_{0} that obeys the assumptions of Theorems 2 and 4 on H0H_{0}. As mentioned above, it is easy to construct initial data set analogously on H¯0\underline{H}_{0} so that the full set of assumptions of Theorems 2 and 4 are satisfied.

5. The Preliminary Estimates

We now turn to the proof Theorem 5, which will form the content of Sections 5-8. In this section, we derive the necessary preliminary estimates. In Section 6 (see Proposition 15), we will prove the bound

∑i≤3𝒪i,2≤C⁡(𝒪i​n​i);\sum_{i\leq 3}\mathcal{O}_{i,2}\leq C(\mathcal{O}_{ini});

in Section 7 (see Proposition 25), we will prove

𝒪~4,2≤C⁡(𝒪i​n​i)​(1+ℛ);\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{4,2}\leq C(\mathcal{O}_{ini})(1+\mathcal{R});

and in Section 8 (see Proposition 32), we will derive the estimate

ℛ≤C⁡(𝒪i​n​i,ℛi​n​i).\mathcal{R}\leq C(\mathcal{O}_{ini},\mathcal{R}_{ini}).

Combining these estimates then imply the conclusion of Theorem 5.

We now begin with the preliminary estimates. All estimates in this section will be proved under the following bootstrap assumption:

∑i≤1𝒪i,∞+∑i≤2𝒪i,4+∑i≤3𝒪i,2≤Δ1,\sum_{i\leq 1}\mathcal{O}_{i,\infty}+\sum_{i\leq 2}\mathcal{O}_{i,4}+\sum_{i\leq 3}\mathcal{O}_{i,2}\leq\Delta_{1}, (A1)

where Δ1\Delta_{1} is a constant that will be chosen later.

Using the estimates for the metric γ\gamma in Proposition 2, we have the following Sobolev embedding theorem:

There exists ϵ0=ϵ0​(Δ1)\epsilon_{0}=\epsilon_{0}(\Delta_{1}) such that as long as ϵ≤ϵ0\epsilon\leq\epsilon_{0}, we have

and

for any tensor ϕ\phi tangential to the spheres Su,u¯S_{u,\underline{u}}. Combining the above estimates, we also have

‖ϕ‖L∞​(Su,u¯)≤C​∑i=02‖∇iϕ‖L2​(Su,u¯).||\phi||_{L^{\infty}(S_{u,\underline{u}})}\leq C\sum_{i=0}^{2}||\nabla^{i}\phi||_{L^{2}(S_{u,\underline{u}})}.
Proof.

By (35) in the proof of Proposition 2, |γA​B​(u,u¯)−γA​B​(0,0)||\gamma_{AB}(u,\underline{u})-\gamma_{AB}(0,0)| can be made arbitrarily small by choosing ϵ\epsilon to be small. Therefore, the isoperimetric constant

I⁡(Su,u¯)=supUmin⁡{Area​(U),Area​(Uc)}Perimeter​(∂U)I(S_{u,\underline{u}})=\sup_{U}\frac{\min\{\mbox{Area}(U),\mbox{Area}(U^{c})\}}{\mbox{Perimeter}(\partial U)}

on every sphere Su,u¯S_{u,\underline{u}} is controlled2525 25 This argument is standard. Once the isoperimetric constants are uniformly controlled, the Sobolev embedding theorem follows from Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 in [5] and the fact that the volume of Su,u¯S_{u,\underline{u}} is bounded uniformly above and below. ∎

Recall the schematic notation

ψ∈{η,η¯},ψH∈{tr​χ,χ^,ω},ψH¯∈{tr​χ¯,χ¯^,ω¯}.\psi\in\{\eta,\underline{\eta}\},\quad\psi_{H}\in\{\mbox{tr}\chi,\hat{\chi},\omega\},\quad\psi_{\underline{H}}\in\{\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi},\hat{\underline{\chi}},\underline{\omega}\}.

we get the following schematic formula for repeated commutations (see [19]):

Proposition 9.

Suppose ∇4ϕ=F0\nabla_{4}\phi=F_{0} for some tensors ϕ\phi and F0F_{0}. Let FiF_{i} be the tensor defined by ∇4∇i​ϕ=Fi\nabla_{4}\nabla^{i}\phi=F_{i}. Then

5.5. General Elliptic Estimates for Hodge Systems

We recall the definition of the divergence and curl of a symmetric covariant tensor of rank r+1r+1:

(div ​ϕ)A1​…​Ar=∇BϕB​A1​…​Ar,(\mbox{div }\phi)_{A_{1}...A_{r}}=\nabla^{B}\phi_{BA_{1}...A_{r}},
(curl ​ϕ)A1​…​Ar=ϵ/B​C∇BϕC​A1​…​Ar,(\mbox{curl }\phi)_{A_{1}...A_{r}}={\epsilon}\mkern-8.0mu/\,^{BC}\nabla_{B}\phi_{CA_{1}...A_{r}},

where ϵ/{\epsilon}\mkern-8.0mu/\, is the volume form associated to the metric γ\gamma. Recall also that the trace is defined to be

(t​r​ϕ)A1​…​Ar−1=(γ−1)B​C​ϕB​C​A1​…​Ar−1.(tr\phi)_{A_{1}...A_{r-1}}=(\gamma^{-1})^{BC}\phi_{BCA_{1}...A_{r-1}}.

The following elliptic estimate is standard (see for example Lemmas 2.2.2, 2.2.3 in [6] or Lemmas 7.1, 7.2, 7.3 in [5]):

Proposition 10.

Let ϕ\phi be a symmetric rr covariant tensor on a 2-sphere (𝕊2,γ)(\mathbb{S}^{2},\gamma) satisfying

div ​ϕ=f,curl ​ϕ=g,t​r​ϕ=h.\mbox{div }\phi=f,\quad\mbox{curl }\phi=g,\quad tr\phi=h.

Suppose also that

∑i≤2‖∇iK‖L2​(S)<∞.\sum_{i\leq 2}||\nabla^{i}K||_{L^{2}(S)}<\infty.

Then for i≤4i\leq 4, there exists a constant CEC_{E} depending only on ∑i≤2‖∇iK‖L2​(S)\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq 2}||\nabla^{i}K||_{L^{2}(S)} such that

‖∇iϕ‖L2​(S)≤CE​(∑j=0i−1(||∇jf||L2​(S)+‖∇jg‖L2​(S)+|​|∇jh||L2​(S)+||∇jϕ||L2​(S))).||\nabla^{i}\phi||_{L^{2}(S)}\leq C_{E}(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}(||\nabla^{j}f||_{L^{2}(S)}+||\nabla^{j}g||_{L^{2}(S)}+||\nabla^{j}h||_{L^{2}(S)}+||{\nabla^{j}}\phi||_{L^{2}(S)})).

For the special case that ϕ\phi is a symmetric traceless 2-tensor, we only need to know its divergence:

Proposition 11.

Suppose ϕ\phi is a symmetric traceless 2-tensor satisfying

div ​ϕ=f.\mbox{div }\phi=f.

Suppose moreover that

∑i≤2‖∇iK‖L2​(S)<∞.\sum_{i\leq 2}||\nabla^{i}K||_{L^{2}(S)}<\infty.

Then for i≤4i\leq 4, there exists a constant CEC_{E} depending only on ∑i≤2‖∇iK‖L2​(S)\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq 2}||\nabla^{i}K||_{L^{2}(S)} such that

‖∇iϕ‖L2​(S)≤CE​(∑j=0i−1(‖∇jf‖L2​(S)+||∇jϕ||L2​(S))).||\nabla^{i}\phi||_{L^{2}(S)}\leq C_{E}(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}(||\nabla^{j}f||_{L^{2}(S)}+||{\nabla^{j}}\phi||_{L^{2}(S)})).
Proof.

This follows from Proposition 10 and the fact that

curl ϕ=∗f.\mbox{curl }\phi=^{*}f.

6. Estimates for the Ricci Coefficients via Transport Equations

In this section, we prove L2L^{2} estimates for the Ricci coefficients and their first, second and third derivatives. We will assume bounds for ℛ\mathcal{R} and 𝒪~4,2\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{4,2} and show that for ϵ0\epsilon_{0} chosen to be sufficiently small, ∑i≤3𝒪i,2\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq 3}\mathcal{O}_{i,2} is likewise bounded. In order to achieve this, we continue to work under the bootstrap assumption (A1) and will show that the constant in (A1) can in fact be improved (see Proposition 15).

Recall that we will use the following notation: ψ∈{η,η¯}\psi\in\{\eta,\underline{\eta}\}, ψH¯∈{tr​χ¯,χ¯^,ω¯}\psi_{\underline{H}}\in\{\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi},\hat{\underline{\chi}},\underline{\omega}\} and ψH∈{tr​χ,χ^,ω}\psi_{H}\in\{\mbox{tr}\chi,\hat{\chi},\omega\}.

We first show bounds for ψ\psi.

Proposition 12.

Assume

ℛ<∞.\mathcal{R}<\infty.

Then there exists ϵ0=ϵ0​(Δ1,ℛ)\epsilon_{0}=\epsilon_{0}(\Delta_{1},\mathcal{R}) such that whenever ϵ≤ϵ0\epsilon\leq\epsilon_{0},

∑i≤3𝒪i,2​[ψ]≤C⁡(𝒪i​n​i),\sum_{i\leq 3}\mathcal{O}_{i,2}[\psi]\leq C(\mathcal{O}_{ini}),

i.e., the bounds depends only on the initial data norm 𝒪i​n​i\mathcal{O}_{ini}. In particular, C⁡(𝒪i​n​i)C(\mathcal{O}_{ini}) is independent of Δ1\Delta_{1}.

Proof.

We first estimate η\eta, the estimates for η¯\underline{\eta} are similar after we replace uu with u¯\underline{u} and 33 with 44. Using the null structure equations, we have a schematic equation of the type

∇4η=β+ψH​ψ.\nabla_{4}\eta=\beta+\psi_{H}\psi.

We also commute the null structure equations with angular derivatives to get

∇4∇i​η=∑i1+i2+i3=i∇i1ψi2​∇i3β+∑i1+i2+i3+i4=i∇i1ψi2​∇i3ψ​∇i4ψH.\nabla_{4}\nabla^{i}\eta=\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}=i}\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi^{i_{2}}\nabla^{i_{3}}\beta+\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}+i_{4}=i}\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi^{i_{2}}\nabla^{i_{3}}\psi\nabla^{i_{4}}\psi_{H}. (39)

By Proposition 5, in order to estimate ‖∇iη‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S)||\nabla^{i}\eta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}, it suffices to estimate the initial data and the ||⋅||Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S)||\cdot||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)} norm of the right hand side (39). Using the bootstrap assumption, we will show that the right hand side is bounded in a weighted Lu¯2L^{2}_{\underline{u}} norm. This in turns imply via an application of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that the Lu¯1L^{1}_{\underline{u}} norm is also bounded. We now turn to the details.

We first estimate the curvature term

∑i1+i2+i3≤3∇i1ψi2​∇i3β.\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}\leq 3}\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi^{i_{2}}\nabla^{i_{3}}\beta.

For the terms such that at most 11 derivative falling on ψ\psi, the bootstrap assumption (A1) allows us to control ∑i≤1‖∇iψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L∞​(S)\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq 1}\|\nabla^{i}\psi\|_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)} by Δ1\Delta_{1}. We then need to control ∑i≤3∇iβ\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq 3}\nabla^{i}\beta in Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S)L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S). By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, since the Lu¯2L^{2}_{\underline{u}} norm of f​(u¯)−1f(\underline{u})^{-1} is smaller than ϵ\epsilon, we can bound this by ∑i≤3∇iβ\displaystyle\sum_{i\leq 3}\nabla^{i}\beta in the weighted L2L^{2} norms. More precisely, we have

‖∑i1≤1,i2≤3,i3≤3∇i1ψi2​∇i3β‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S)≤C⁡(∑i1≤1,i2≤3‖∇i1ψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L∞​(S)i2)​(∑i3≤3‖f⁡(u¯)​∇i3β‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S))≤C⁡(∑i1≤1,i2≤3‖∇i1ψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L∞​(S)i2)​(∑i3≤3‖f⁡(u¯)​∇i3β‖Lu∞​Lu¯2​L2​(S))||f​(u¯)−1||Lu∞​Lu¯2​L∞​(S)≤C​ϵ​(1+Δ1)3​ℛ.\begin{split}&||\sum_{i_{1}\leq 1,i_{2}\leq 3,i_{3}\leq 3}\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi^{i_{2}}\nabla^{i_{3}}\beta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}\\ \leq&C(\sum_{i_{1}\leq 1,i_{2}\leq 3}||\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi||^{i_{2}}_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)})(\sum_{i_{3}\leq 3}||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{i_{3}}\beta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)})\\ {\leq}&C(\sum_{i_{1}\leq 1,i_{2}\leq 3}||\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi||^{i_{2}}_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)})(\sum_{i_{3}\leq 3}||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{i_{3}}\beta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)})||f(\underline{u})^{-1}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)}\\ \leq&C\epsilon(1+\Delta_{1})^{3}\mathcal{R}{.}\end{split} (40)

For the term where exactly 22 derivatives fall on ψ\psi (notice that this is the highest number of derivatives that can fall on ψ\psi), we control ∇2ψ\nabla^{2}\psi in Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S)L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S) by Δ1\Delta_{1} (using (A1)). More precisely,

‖∇2ψ​β‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S)≤C​‖∇2ψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S)​‖β‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L∞​(S)≤C​‖∇2ψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S)​(∑i≤2‖∇iβ‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S))≤C​‖∇2ψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S)​(∑i≤2‖f⁡(u¯)​∇iβ‖Lu∞​Lu¯2​L∞​(S))||f​(u¯)−1||Lu∞​Lu¯2​L∞​(S)≤C​ϵ​Δ1​ℛ.\begin{split}&||\nabla^{2}\psi\beta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}\\ \leq&C||\nabla^{2}\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}||\beta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)}\\ \leq&C||\nabla^{2}\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}(\sum_{i\leq 2}||\nabla^{i}\beta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)})\\ \leq&C||\nabla^{2}\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}(\sum_{i\leq 2}||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{i}\beta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)})||f(\underline{u})^{-1}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)}\\ \leq&C\epsilon\Delta_{1}\mathcal{R}.\end{split} (41)

Combining (40) and (41), we have

‖∑i1+i2+i3≤3∇i1ψi2​∇i3β‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S)≤C​ϵ​(1+Δ1)3​ℛ.||\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}\leq 3}\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi^{i_{2}}\nabla^{i_{3}}\beta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}\leq C\epsilon(1+\Delta_{1})^{3}\mathcal{R}.

We then estimate the second term in (39). We separate the terms where more derivatives fall on ψH\psi_{H} and those where more derivatives fall on ψ\psi:

‖∑i1+i2+i3+i4≤3∇i1ψi2​∇i3ψ​∇i4ψH‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S)≤C⁡(∑i1≤1,1≤i2≤4‖∇i1ψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L∞​(S)i2)​(∑i3≤3‖∇i3ψH‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S))+C⁡(1+‖ψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L∞​(S))​(∑i1≤3‖∇i1ψ‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S))​(∑i2≤1‖∇i2ψH‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L∞​(S))≤C​Δ1​(1+Δ1)3​(∑i≤3‖∇iψH‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L2​(S)+∑i≤1‖∇iψH‖Lu∞​Lu¯1​L∞​(S))≤C​Δ1​(1+Δ1)3​‖f​(u¯)−1‖Lu∞​Lu¯2​L∞​(S)×(∑i≤3‖f⁡(u¯)​∇iψH‖Lu∞​Lu¯2​L2​(S)+∑i≤1‖f⁡(u¯)​∇iψH‖Lu∞​Lu¯2​L∞​(S))≤C​Δ12​(1+Δ1)3​ϵ.\begin{split}&||\sum_{i_{1}+i_{2}+i_{3}+i_{4}\leq 3}\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi^{i_{2}}\nabla^{i_{3}}\psi\nabla^{i_{4}}\psi_{H}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}\\ \leq&C(\sum_{i_{1}\leq 1,{1\leq}i_{2}\leq 4}||\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)}^{i_{2}})(\sum_{i_{3}\leq 3}||\nabla^{i_{3}}\psi_{H}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)})\\ &+C(1+||\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)})(\sum_{i_{1}\leq 3}||\nabla^{i_{1}}\psi||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)})(\sum_{i_{2}\leq 1}||\nabla^{i_{2}}\psi_{H}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)})\\ \leq&C\Delta_{1}(1+\Delta_{1})^{3}(\sum_{{i}\leq 3}||\nabla^{{i}}\psi_{H}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}+\sum_{{i}\leq 1}||\nabla^{{i}}\psi_{H}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{1}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)})\\ \leq&C\Delta_{1}(1+\Delta_{1})^{3}||f(\underline{u})^{-1}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)}\\ &\times(\sum_{{i}\leq 3}||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{{i}}\psi_{H}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}+\sum_{{i}\leq 1}||f(\underline{u})\nabla^{{i}}\psi_{H}||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{2}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)})\\ \leq&C\Delta_{1}^{2}(1+\Delta_{1})^{3}\epsilon.\end{split} (42)

Hence, by Proposition 5, we have

∑i≤3‖∇iη‖Lu∞​Lu¯∞​L2​(S)≤C⁡(𝒪i​n​i)+C​ϵ​(Δ12​(1+Δ1)3+ℛ​(1+Δ1)3)≤C⁡(𝒪i​n​i),\sum_{i\leq 3}||\nabla^{i}\eta||_{L^{\infty}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{2}(S)}\leq C(\mathcal{O}_{ini})+C\epsilon(\Delta_{1}^{2}(1+\Delta_{1})^{3}+\mathcal{R}(1+\Delta_{1})^{3})\leq C(\mathcal{O}_{ini}),

after choosing ϵ\epsilon to be sufficiently small. Similarly, we consider the equation for ∇3∇i​η¯\nabla_{3}\nabla^{i}\underline{\eta} to get

∎

We now move to the terms that we denote by ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}}, i.e., tr​χ¯\mbox{tr}\underline{\chi}, χ¯^\hat{\underline{\chi}} and ω¯\underline{\omega}. All of them obey a ∇4\nabla_{4} equation. Unlike the previous estimates for ψ\psi, the initial data for the quantities ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}} are not in Lu∞L^{\infty}_{u}. We will therefore prove only a bound for ψH¯\psi_{\underline{H}} in the weighted norm ||f(u)⋅||Lu2​Lu¯∞​L∞​(S)||f(u)\cdot||_{L^{2}_{u}L^{\infty}_{\underline{u}}L^{\infty}(S)}.

Proposition 13.

Assume

ℛ<∞,𝒪~4,2<∞.\mathcal{R}<\infty,\quad\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{4,2}<\infty.
